clinicalPearls: A restrictive strabismus in which elevation of the eye is limited in adduction owing to impaired free movement of the superior oblique tendon through the trochlea
Elevation improves in abduction, giving a characteristic V-pattern and a positive forced duction test in adduction
May be congenital or acquired; acquired forms can follow trauma, sinus or orbital surgery, or inflammation of the trochlear region
There is usually little or no primary-position deviation, and a downshoot on adduction (an inverted-Y or divergence in upgaze) may be seen
A palpable or audible click on movement suggests an intermittent form as the tendon catches at the trochlea
Congenital cases are often stable and may improve spontaneously; painful acquired inflammatory cases can respond to anti-inflammatory treatment
Surgery, typically a superior oblique weakening procedure, is reserved for a significant hypotropia in primary position or an anomalous head posture
reference.pathophysiology: Brown syndrome results from mechanical restriction of the superior oblique tendon-trochlea complex, preventing the tendon from sliding freely and thereby limiting elevation of the eye when it is adducted. Congenital forms involve a structurally short or inelastic tendon or an abnormal trochlear apparatus, while acquired forms follow inflammation, scarring, trauma or surgery around the trochlea that impairs tendon excursion. Because the restriction is mechanical, forced ductions are positive and elevation is worst in adduction, where the tendon pulley effect is greatest, but improves in abduction. Intermittent catching of a swollen or nodular tendon at the trochlea can produce a click and variable limitation.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles
additionalInvestigations: Orthoptic assessment of ductions, versions and pattern deviations
Forced duction testing to confirm mechanical restriction
Assessment of head posture and primary-position deviation
Orbital imaging when an acquired or inflammatory cause is suspected
Inflammatory markers or systemic screen in suspected inflammatory Brown syndrome
redFlags: Painful acquired restriction suggesting active trochlear inflammation or a systemic inflammatory disorder
Progressive or fluctuating restriction requiring imaging to exclude an orbital lesion
A large primary-position hypotropia with anomalous head posture affecting development
Recent trauma or surgery indicating possible entrapment
reference.prognosis: Congenital Brown syndrome is often stable and can improve without intervention, and acquired inflammatory forms may resolve with treatment; surgery is effective for persistent, functionally significant cases though overcorrection can occur.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for an inferior oblique palsy despite the different pattern
Failing to perform forced duction testing and missing the mechanical restriction
Overlooking an inflammatory or orbital cause in acquired cases
Operating on a mild congenital case that would have improved spontaneously
references: Taylor & Hoyt's Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Observe congenital cases without significant head posture, hypotropia or amblyopia, as many are stable or improve spontaneously
Treat acquired inflammatory forms with anti-inflammatory therapy, using systemic or local peritrochlear corticosteroids and non-steroidal agents to relieve pain and restore tendon excursion
Identify and treat any underlying inflammatory, sinus or orbital cause driving acquired restriction
Correct refractive error on cycloplegic refraction and treat amblyopia in affected children
Reserve strabismus surgery (superior oblique tendon weakening or lengthening) for persistent, functionally significant restriction with abnormal head posture or primary-position hypotropia
Undertake serial orthoptic monitoring of ductions, versions, pattern deviation and head posture, and counsel on the risk of postoperative overcorrection
Refer to paediatric ophthalmology and strabismus services for assessment and operative planning
